segments.text: We are {team_name}: {others} and me, Yash Goel.
Our dataset is GOES-16's lightning mapper. We sampled one file every 5 minutes for summer 2024, {flashes_k} thousand flashes, binned to a 1 degree grid by hour of day, in UTC and local solar time.
First, where. Land dominates: {land_share:.0f} percent of flashes, with hotspots in Florida, Colombia and the Amazon.
Second, when. Across the hemisphere lightning peaks at {all_peak}; 1 to 6 PM holds {all_afternoon:.0f} percent of all flashes.
Third, land against ocean. Land peaks at {land_peak}, ocean at {ocean_peak}, and {ocean_night:.0f} percent of ocean flashes happen at night.

Fourth, each cell's peak hour. {land_aft:.0f} percent of land cells peak in the afternoon, {ocean_night_cells:.0f} percent of ocean cells at night. The Great Plains are a night patch inside a continent.
Fifth, three regions. The Southeast peaks at {se_peak}, the Amazon at {amazon_peak}, but the Plains at {plains_peak}, with {plains_night:.0f} percent of their lightning at night.
Sixth, four hours on one scale. At 3 PM the continents light up. At 3 AM the lightning sits over the sea and the Plains.

segments.item: Title of the graph and the question
segments.text: Our title: {title} Our question: at what hour does lightning peak over land and ocean, and where does it strike at night?

segments.item: Current progress on the final dynamic graph
segments.text: Our D3 prototype: drag or play the hour and watch land light up by afternoon and the sea by night. Toggle local solar time to UTC. Click two cells to compare their daily curves, or jump to Florida, the Plains and Maracaibo. Left: polish and the write-up.
